nameStory: Dune tansy gets its name from its coastal habitat – it thrives in the sandy dunes along New England's shoreline. The word 'tansy' comes from the Greek 'athanatos' meaning immortal, referring to the long-lasting nature of tansy flowers when dried.
description: Dune tansy is a hardy coastal wildflower that looks like a miniature version of its inland cousin, common tansy. This low-growing perennial reaches just 1-2 feet tall and spreads by underground stems to form patches in sandy soil. Its deeply divided, feathery leaves give it a delicate appearance, while clusters of small yellow button-like flowers top the stems from summer into fall.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small bright yellow button-shaped flower heads about ¼ inch across, packed together in flat-topped clusters. Unlike daisies, these lack white petals – they're all tiny yellow disc flowers that feel slightly fuzzy to touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Finely divided, feathery leaves that feel soft and slightly fuzzy, with a strong aromatic scent when crushed – somewhat bitter and camphor-like. The leaves are deeply cut into many small segments, giving them a lacy appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, compact plant rarely exceeding 2 feet tall, often forming spreading patches through underground runners. Much shorter and more prostrate than common tansy, appearing almost shrub-like in coastal winds.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Sturdy, somewhat woody at the base, often with a reddish tinge. Stems feel firm and slightly ridged when rolled between your fingers.

habitat: Dune tansy is found exclusively in coastal environments, particularly in sandy dunes, beach edges, and salt marshes along New England's Atlantic coastline. It thrives in well-drained sandy soils and can tolerate salt spray and harsh coastal winds. Look for it growing alongside beach grass, seaside goldenrod, and other salt-tolerant plants.

seasonality.spring: New feathery leaves emerge in late spring, appearing silvery-green and very aromatic when the weather warms.
seasonality.summer: Bright yellow button flowers appear in mid to late summer, creating showy flat-topped clusters that attract butterflies and bees.
seasonality.fall: Flowers persist into early fall, eventually turning brown but often remaining on the plant. Leaves may take on reddish tints.
seasonality.winter: Stems die back to woody bases, leaving dried flower heads that may persist. Look for low, woody stem remnants in the sand.

funFact: Dune tansy is so rare in New England that it's been spotted only 7 times by naturalists – making it one of the region's botanical unicorns! This scarcity is partly due to coastal development destroying its specialized dune habitat.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with common tansy, but dune tansy is much shorter (under 2 feet vs. 3-4 feet), grows only in coastal areas, and has a more compact, spreading growth habit. If you're not within sight or smell of the ocean, it's probably common tansy.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'dune tansy,' this plant is actually quite different from the common tansy that many people know as a garden herb or roadside weed. The extreme rarity of dune tansy in New England makes every sighting valuable to botanists tracking coastal plant communities.
compareHints: Compared to common tansy, dune tansy is much shorter and more compact, adapted for harsh coastal conditions rather than inland meadows. Unlike feverfew (another Tanacetum), dune tansy lacks white daisy-like petals and has much more finely divided, aromatic foliage. The coastal habitat alone usually distinguishes it from its inland relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Tansy differs from its cousin feverfew by having purely yellow button flowers instead of feverfew's white daisy-like blooms with yellow centers.
Unlike its cousin tansy which has button-like yellow flowers with no white petals, feverfew always has the classic white daisy appearance.
